coverage.explain: Reads, writes, syncs and opens of files: data files, redo and undo logs, binary logs, temporary files.
coverage.label: File I/O

coverage.explain: Row operations through the storage engine interface (fetch, insert, update, delete). Each wait covers the whole engine call, so file I/O and internal lock waits inside it are counted here and again under their own events.
coverage.label: Table I/O

coverage.explain: Table-level lock requests made through the storage engine interface.

coverage.explain: Network reads and writes on client and replication connections.
coverage.label: Socket I/O

notes: Some wait classes are not instrumented (mutexes 0 of 173 on, read/write locks 0 of 33 on, shared/exclusive locks 0 of 1 on, condition waits 0 of 79 on, socket i/o 0 of 3 on), so their waits are not in this report. No mutex or rwlock waits here never means no contention.
MariaDB turns the metadata lock instrument (wait/lock/metadata/sql/mdl) off by default; MySQL turns it on.

Wait time is summed across all threads, background threads included, so it can exceed the wall-clock window. Table I/O includes the file I/O and internal lock waits inside each call, which are counted again under their own events, so the classes are never added up.
InnoDB asynchronous I/O (read-ahead, page cleaner writes) is timed only for submitting the request, so its latency is understated. Bytes are exact (see I/O).
Since server start covers 13 min 55 s of uptime; the longest single wait (max) is since start too, never per window.
